query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In chromium-bearing steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, enhancing the density of grain boundaries via severe plastic deformation accelerates Cr diffusion to the surface, thereby promoting the rapid formation of a continuous, chromium‐rich passive oxide film that retards corrosive dissolution through grain-boundary–controlled diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional steel alloy with sufficient Cr (and typically Ni) content exhibiting a coarse-grained microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply processing (e.g., high-pressure torsion or other severe plastic deformation) to produce an ultrafine-grained (UFG) version of the same steel, increasing the grain boundary density.
generation.conditions: Exposure in controlled environments that mimic chemical-processing and nuclear conditions, such as in aqueous solutions containing chloride ions or in molten salt mixtures maintained at moderately high temperature, under constant temperature, pressure, and chemical composition.
generation.structural_mediator: A passivation film enriched in chromium formed by enhanced diffusion along the increased grain boundary network.
generation.mechanism: The UFG microstructure offers a high density of grain boundaries that serve as fast diffusion pathways for Cr atoms, leading to rapid restoration of a Cr-enriched oxide layer that counteracts local dissolution and impedes corrosion. Additionally, micro-galvanic effects between different phases may help sustain the passivation film by directing corrosion to less critical regions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to coarse-grained steel, the UFG steel will exhibit a significantly lower corrosion current density, a more stable passivation behavior (less pitting and lower Icorr), and XPS measurements will show a higher concentration of Cr in the passive layer under identical corrosive conditions.
generation.baseline: The same steel alloy in its conventional, coarse-grained form without additional grain refinement.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be valid for steels with adequate Cr (and supporting alloying elements like Ni) and in environments that are moderately corrosive (e.g., typical chloride-bearing solutions and molten salts at temperatures up to about 650 °C). Extremely aggressive environments (e.g., with high impurity levels or mechanical abrasion) may obscure the passivation benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between the degree of grain refinement and the resulting improvement in passivation is uncertain, as is the threshold level of ultrafineness required to achieve a measurable benefit in all relevant environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel samples with identical chemical composition: one with a conventional coarse-grained microstructure and the other processed to achieve an ultrafine-grained (UFG) structure via severe plastic deformation. Expose both sets to a simulated corrosive environment (e.g., 0.6 M NaCl solution at elevated temperature or molten salt at 450 °C) under identical conditions. Use electrochemical techniques to measure corrosion rates and surface analytical methods to assess the composition and uniformity of the passive film.
measurements: Corrosion current density (Icorr) and open circuit potential via polarization curves
Surface film composition and thickness using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
Surface potential mapping using scanning Kelvin probe
SEM (and/or AFM) imaging for local pitting and corrosion morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the UFG steel does not show a statistically significant decrease in corrosion rate and fails to exhibit enhanced Cr enrichment in the passive film (as compared to the coarse-grained baseline) under the test conditions, then the hypothesized mechanism of grain-boundary–enhanced passivation would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy. Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion.

Severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques enable the fabrication of ultrafine-grained (UFG) or nanocrystalline (NC) materials in bulk forms suitable for load-carrying structural applications []. With the advent of SPD, there has been an increasing demand to clarify the effect of UFG/NC formation on corrosion from a practical viewpoint, especially with regard to the classic topic of the effect of grain size on corrosion [,]. Among the various materials investigated to date, stainless steels exhibited mostly improved corrosion resistance by forming UFG structures by SPD [,,,,,,,]. The enhanced corrosion resistance of UFG/NC SSs compared with coarse-grained (CG) materials has been mostly attributed to greater Cr enrichment in the passivation film [,,,,,,,,], which has been validated experimentally by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) [] and recently by Cs-corrected scanning-transmission electron microscopy (STEM) [,]. Two possibilities for the enhanced Cr enrichment in the passivation film of UFG/NC materials have been proposed.
